Let's dive into Chapter 6—Navigating the “Monitor” and the Importance of Progress.
Imagine you’ve got this internal dashboard running in the background—a kind of “monitor” that’s always asking, “Am I moving closer to what really matters to me?” This monitor quietly tracks your progress toward your goals, sending little signals about when to keep going... and when it might be time to let up or even give up.
Here’s why that matters: when you can actually see your progress—even if it’s just a little bit at a time—motivation and hope stick around. But if your monitor senses you’re stuck, or that you’re up against the same wall over and over, that’s when frustration creeps in. And if it goes on too long, burnout can follow.
The tricky part? This monitor responds not just to real, obvious changes, but also to what you *think* is happening. Take a parent working hard for a peaceful family routine. Maybe bedtime is a little calmer this week, and that feels encouraging. But if setbacks start piling up—like tantrums, missed appointments, or just never feeling appreciated—the monitor might start whispering, “Is all this effort really worth it?” That’s when exhaustion can set in, or maybe you just want to check out altogether.
So, how do you work *with* your monitor instead of against it?
First, break those big, overwhelming goals into smaller, visible steps. And don’t wait for huge victories—celebrate the little wins, even if they seem minor.
Second, try tracking your progress in ways you can actually see. Maybe you keep a journal, use a checklist, or put up a visual reminder on the fridge. When you can see movement, it’s easier to stay motivated.
Third, when setbacks happen—and they will—try to reframe them. Instead of seeing obstacles as proof you’ve failed, treat them as information. What’s this telling you? Maybe it’s time to adjust your approach.
And finally, ask for feedback and support. Sometimes the people around you notice progress you might have missed. Just hearing, “Hey, I can tell you’re making an effort,” can make all the difference.
This way of working with your monitor is especially important in situations where results are slow or hard to spot—like caregiving, healing, or advocacy. By making progress visible and meaningful, you keep your internal monitor satisfied... and avoid that draining feeling of endless, unrewarded effort.
